answerBody:
The final rule should make federal preemption the governing default when a local wireline right-of-way approval is delayed beyond a defined shot clock or conditioned on above-cost charges, while preserving a clear rebuttal path for genuinely unusual projects. The default should not be “local control unless the provider proves a specific rule blocks service,” because that standard waits until the damage is done and rewards the jurisdictions least willing to give a timely yes or no.

The statutory anchor is Section 253 of the Communications Act. Subsection (a) bars state or local legal requirements that prohibit or have the effect of prohibiting telecommunications service; subsections (b) and (c) preserve public-safety authority, right-of-way management, and fair, reasonable, competitively neutral, publicly disclosed compensation. The FCC’s August 7, 2026 Federal Register notice proposes a rebuttable presumption that failure to process all required right-of-way authorizations within 120 days effectively prohibits service, and proposes limiting fees to a reasonable approximation of actual, direct right-of-way management costs. That is the right structure: not field preemption of trenching, traffic control, restoration, historic preservation, or safety review, but a federal default against delay and rent extraction.

The practical reason is that broadband deployment is a network investment problem. A provider cannot efficiently plan crews, financing, pole work, materials, and customer acquisition if every municipality can turn an application into an indefinite negotiation. Even a fee or delay in one locality can strand routes that connect other localities. The Ninth Circuit’s 2020 City of Portland decision upheld the FCC’s view that cost-anchored fees can be a lawful way to identify unreasonable local charges, recognizing that unconstrained fees can leave providers at the mercy of monopoly control over rights-of-way. That logic is stronger for wireline builds, where ducts, poles, crossings, and streets are unavoidable inputs.

The strongest counterargument is serious: cities and counties maintain crowded, hazardous public corridors, and local associations including the National League of Cities, National Association of Counties, United States Conference of Mayors, and NATOA argued in September 2026 that the proposal could undermine public safety and taxpayer property. They are right that a missed deadline should not automatically authorize unsafe excavation, and that small governments may need flexibility for incomplete applications, emergencies, seasonal limits, or unusually complex work.

But that supports a rebuttable federal presumption, not a local-control default. The final rule should toll the clock for materially incomplete applications, allow written extensions tied to objective safety or engineering needs, and permit cost recovery with records. It should also avoid deemed-granted approvals for construction that would create immediate safety risks; the remedy can be expedited federal or court preemption of the offending delay or charge. The conclusion-changing evidence would be a robust record showing that ordinary local timelines and fees rarely change build decisions and that federal shot clocks materially increase unsafe construction. On the present record, the better default is federal preemption of unjustified delay and above-cost exactions.
rationale: The answer is based on current FCC proposal materials, Section 253’s statutory structure, relevant City of Portland precedent, and recent local-government opposition filings. It chooses and defends a governing default while addressing counterarguments and uncertainty.
